## The Socratic tutor as an ACP agent

This annex explains how to install and run the course's Socratic tutor as an
**external agent** in Zed — the setup the instructor uses in the classroom
demos. It is a companion to
[appendix-local-llm.qmd](appendix-local-llm.qmd), which covers the plain local
model (Ling-3.0-tiny) inside the built-in agent. The tutor version is a separate
Python runner that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) to Zed and gives the
model a **fully controlled system prompt**.

## Why an ACP agent and not the built-in agent?

The tutor is normally started from an `AGENTS.md` persona inside Zed's built-in
agent (ai-tutor.qmd). That works, but with a constraint you cannot remove with
the built-in agent: **Zed always prefixes a large system prompt** of its own
(communication rules, formatting, detailed tool use — on the order of 3–4k
tokens), and `AGENTS.md` can only be *appended* to that scaffolding, never
replace it. For a 4–9B local model this scaffolding is noise that steers it off
course (tool-format confusion, answer leakage, repetition).

An **external ACP agent** removes that constraint. Zed only hosts the
conversation thread; the agent owns the model call, the system prompt, and the
tools. The prompt that reaches the model is exactly what the agent sends —
**no default, no scaffolding**. What the model gets comes from the project you
have open in Zed:

- `<workspace>/AGENTS.<model>.md` — used when that model is selected;
- otherwise `<workspace>/AGENTS.md` — the shared base;
- if neither exists, no system message at all.

Because the variant *replaces* the base, each `AGENTS.<model>.md` you deploy is
a **full** system prompt. The runner adds two extras on top of the prompt
control:

- **read-only, scoped tools** — the model can read the course material
  (`Courses/*.qmd`, the rendered book) and the files of your open project, with
  bounded paths (absolute paths and `..` are refused); there is no write tool;
- **clickable citations** — references the model writes as `fichier.qmd:line`
  and `python:<reference>` come back as links that open the locally served book
  page and the official Python documentation.

What you need, all in the files your instructor distributes:

- the **runner folder** (`Tutor-agent/`, generic and in English — it also
  downloads the tutor models, so it is large);
- the **corpus** (folder holding `Courses/`, `www/`, `sections.json`);
- the **tutor prompts** (pre-assembled `AGENTS*.md` files).

## Installation step by step

### 1. Get the runner and its dependencies

Clone the runner — public repository <https://github.com/fradav/tutor-agent> —
or copy the `Tutor-agent/` folder your instructor distributes, then install
its single Python dependency with `uv`:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/fradav/tutor-agent
cd tutor-agent        # repo folder name (lowercase): keep it in steps 3 and 5
uv sync
```

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+, `uv` (https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), and
`llama-server` from llama.cpp (Homebrew: `brew install llama.cpp`,
**≥ 0.3.0** — the version with router mode).

### 2. Download the tutor models

The runner serves three local models through one `llama-server` router on port
`8025`. Fetch the GGUF weights (resumable; run again to finish):

```bash
uv run python models/fetch_models.py            # all 3 .gguf → models/
uv run python models/fetch_models.py --list     # names + expected sizes
```

About 17 GB of free disk is needed for the three files.

### 3. Point the runner at the course corpus

The corpus is not shipped inside the public `Tutor-agent/` repo — it is
centralized. If the distributed files already contain a `config.local.json`,
skip this step. Otherwise create one in `Tutor-agent/` (it is gitignored) that
redirects the corpus to the folder you received:

```json
{
  "paths": {
    "course_dir": "/path/to/your/distributed/MIASHS-Configuration-Tutorat"
  }
}
```

`course_dir` is the anchor: `Courses/`, `www/` and `sections.json` are resolved
under it.

### 4. Deploy the prompts into your workspace

Create a folder for your tutoring sessions (where you will write and test your
code — this is the workspace you will open in Zed), then copy the prompts into
it:

```bash
cp path/to/distributed/agents/AGENTS.md  ~/tutorat/
cp path/to/distributed/agents/AGENTS.qwen3.5-4B.md   ~/tutorat/   # default model
```

`AGENTS.md` is the shared preamble. Each `AGENTS.<model>.md` is the *full*
prompt for that model, so copy the variants for the models you intend to use
(`AGENTS.ornith-1.5-9B.md`, `AGENTS.gemma-4-E4B.md`). You can always add more
later — no script involved.

### 5. Register the agent in Zed

Add an entry under `agent_servers` in `settings.json` (macOS:
`~/.config/zed/settings.json`), or use *Agent Settings → External Agents → Add
Custom Agent*, which writes the same block:

```json
{
  "agent_servers": {
    "tuteur": {
      "type": "custom",
      "command": ["uv", "run", "--project", "/abs/path/to/Tutor-agent", "python", "/abs/path/to/Tutor-agent/acp_agent.py"]
    }
  }
}
```

Point both paths at your copy of the runner folder. If `uv` is not on Zed's
PATH, use its absolute path (e.g. `/opt/homebrew/bin/uv`). Reload the window.

### 6. Choose the agent and the model in Zed

Open the workspace folder where you deployed the prompts, then:

1. In the Agent panel, `+` shows the external agents — select **tuteur**.
2. Pick the model in the agent's **Modèle** selector — one option per profile:
   `qwen3.5-4B`, `ornith-1.5-9B`, `gemma-4-E4B`. The choice applies when the
   session starts.
3. Start a conversation.

On the first prompt the runner starts the local router it needs (port 8025) and
the docs server (port 8765) that the clickable citations open — no manual
start. For manual control from a terminal:

```bash
uv run run.py start qwen3.5-4B   # ensure the router serves the model
uv run run.py status             # port + served aliases
uv run run.py stop               # stop the managed router
```

## Choosing a model

Start with **qwen3.5-4B**. It is the best overall balance for this tutor: it
keeps the Socratic back-and-forth (asks, does not hand out answers), anchors its
replies to the course pages and cites them, resists inventing content on modest
hardware, and runs comfortably on a laptop (4B class, quantized). There is no
reason to pick another model first.

Pick another model only for a specific reason:

| Model | Size | Use it when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ornith-1.5-9B` | 9B | you have a bit more RAM/VRAM and want a more patient, longer dialogue | its first turns can be verbose |
| `gemma-4-E4B` | 4B | factual accuracy of the course citations matters to you | it can leak "internal notes" into its reply; insist it only writes for you |

Both alternatives are about the same memory-footprint class as the default in
practice; `ornith` is heavier.

A limit that applies to all three: every provided model eventually hands over a
full code block if you insist long enough ("just give me the code"). That is a
known failure mode of this setup, not something a specific model fixes. The
tutor tries to walk you through the reasoning first — cooperate with it: state
what you have tried, let it read your code, keep the "show me, don't tell me"
rule.

Notes:

- `temperature 0.6` is set for all three — deterministic enough, varied enough.
  Do not raise it past ~0.7; the tutor starts to ramble.
- If the model's answer comes back empty or stuck (a known qwen + thinking
  quirk on llama.cpp), just send the prompt again. The runner streams the
  reasoning on its own channel and re-injects it across turns automatically;
  there is no per-model toggle to flip.
